**"The Cleanest Man in Garland County"**

Mace Pruitt, a broke, disgraced former health inspector in a swamp-rotted Arkansas county, stumbles into solving a string of fentanyl murders by obsessively cataloguing restaurant code violations that turn out to be connected to a cartel laundering operation—his unfiltered, spiraling inner monologue cataloguing every cracked floor tile and grease-trap anomaly as if sanitation *is* justice, because to him it literally is. His unlikely wins earn him a cable news following, a consultancy deal, and the worship of a country that loves a blue-collar Sherlock, but the satire bites hardest as we watch, from inside his skull, the precise moment his righteous fixation curdles into the same corruption he exposed—accepting payoffs to *not* notice violations, rationalizing each one in the same obsessive stream that once made him brilliant. The criminal he could never identify is the county sheriff who fed him every lead, grooming Mace from the start as a useful idiot whose downfall was always the exit strategy, and by the final page Mace is dictating his confession into a restaurant complaint form, still believing sanitation scores are the only moral framework that ever made sense in a world this filthy.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Scene-Level Beats for *The Cleanest Man in Garland County*

---

## Beat 1: The Inspection Voice Before It Has a Subject

**What needs to happen:** Before any plot event, the reader must be submerged—fully, uncomfortably—inside Mace Pruitt's monologue. He is cataloguing violations somewhere mundane: his own kitchen, his truck cab, his body in a mirror. Cracked caulk. Mildew bloom on a ceiling tile. The temperature danger zone of a gas station coffee he's holding. Nothing is at stake yet. There is no crime, no career, no fame. There is only a man who cannot stop *scoring the world*.

**The structural function:** This is your thesis scene. It must establish that Mace's obsessive sanitation consciousness is not a professional skill he deploys—it is the substrate of his perception. He does not turn it on; he cannot turn it off. The reader should understand within two pages that this voice is simultaneously the funniest thing they've ever read (the specificity, the absurd granularity, the deadpan moral weight assigned to a grease-trap) and the saddest (because it is clearly a man whose only remaining framework for making sense of a world that discarded him is the one thing he was trained to do). The comedy and the pathos must be *fused*, not alternating.

**Why this must come first:** The entire novel is a single instrument played in different keys. This beat is where you tune the instrument and let the reader hear its timbre before you play any melody. If the inspection voice is introduced *in the context of the mystery*, the reader will code it as a detective's quirk—a gimmick, a Monk-style eccentricity. If it is introduced *before the mystery exists*, in the aimless drift of a broke man with nothing to inspect, it registers as something far more essential and more dangerous: an ontology. The voice must precede the plot so that when the plot arrives, we understand it is the voice that *generates* the plot, not the other way around. Lispector's multiple titles told us that the lens precedes the event. Here, Mace's lens precedes the crime. The deepest trick is that this opening, which seems like pure character work, is actually foreshadowing the ending: a man who can only process reality through inspection forms will, when he finally needs to confess, reach for an inspection form. The instrument doesn't change. Only what it's pointed at.

---

## Beat 2: The Recipe — First Violations, First Body

**What needs to happen:** Mace, scraping by on odd jobs or trying to reclaim some version of his former authority, enters a restaurant—perhaps conducting an unofficial inspection, perhaps dragged there by proximity to a death or a tip. He catalogues the violations with the same compulsive fluency we've already heard. The violations are grotesque, specific, real: a walk-in cooler at 52°F, mouse droppings behind a flour bin, a handwashing sink repurposed for mop water. But threaded among these genuine health horrors are details that don't quite fit the sanitation frame—anomalies in the building, the supply chain, the hours of operation, the money. A fentanyl death has occurred nearby or on the premises. Mace does not recognize the connection. He only sees the violations. He files them, or tries to, with whatever shred of official standing he has left.

**The structural function:** This is procedural realism as Trojan horse, identical in principle to Lispector's poison recipe. The health inspection genre—its jargon, its checklists, its numerical scores—is inherently comic and inherently authoritative. It *anesthetizes*. The reader, like Mace, is lulled into the rhythm of cataloguing, and in that rhythm the actual crime evidence hides in plain sight. You are training the reader to see through Mace's eyes, which means training them to see everything *except* what matters. The first body (or the first death connected to fentanyl) must be present but must *not* be the thing Mace focuses on. His focus is on the cracked floor tile, the expired ServSafe certificate, the condensation pattern that suggests a ventilation failure. The death is context. The violations are text.

**Why this must work this way:** The reader's complicity is essential—and it must be built here. If the reader immediately sees past the violations to the crime, the entire novel collapses into conventional mystery where Mace is a charming but oblivious narrator. Instead, the violations must be so *interesting*, so satisfyingly detailed and revolting, that the reader is seduced into Mace's frame right alongside him. We must genuinely enjoy the inspection. We must find the cracked tile more vivid than the dead addict. This is the trap. Later, when the same cataloguing voice is used to rationalize corruption, the reader will remember this scene and realize they were *already* participating in the same selective attention that makes corruption possible. The recipe, as Lispector knew, makes the cook complicit.

---

## Beat 3: The Violations Become Clues — First Transfiguration

**What needs to happen:** A pattern clicks. Mace notices—or someone (critically: the sheriff) nudges him toward noticing—that the restaurants with the worst violations share structural anomalies that correspond to the fentanyl deaths. Not thematically. *Literally*. The same plumbing contractor. The same landlord. Renovations that created dead spaces in walls. Coolers that run at wrong temperatures because the compressors were replaced with units that serve a different purpose. The violations Mace has been cataloguing are not just failures of hygiene—they are the *physical signatures* of a laundering and distribution operation that has repurposed restaurant infrastructure. The cracked floor tile is cracked because something is stored beneath it. The grease trap backs up because the drainage line was rerouted. Mace sees this, and the inspection voice, which has been comic and melancholy, suddenly sounds like *revelation*.

**The structural function:** This is your defamiliarization beat—the cockroaches becoming statues. The identical data (violations) is re-seen through a new lens (criminal evidence) and the transformation is electrifying. What was banal becomes brilliant. What was pathetic becomes heroic. The key technical challenge is that the prose must not change register dramatically. Mace's voice should sound *almost the same*. He is still cataloguing. He is still assigning scores. But now each violation carries double meaning, and the obsessive specificity that seemed like a symptom of a broken man is revealed as the exact cognitive tool needed to see what no detective, no DEA agent, no journalist could see. The reader's emotion should be the uncanny thrill of watching something familiar become suddenly alien and meaningful—Shklovsky's ostranenie, but earned through accumulated procedural detail rather than lyric estrangement.

**Why this is the hinge:** Everything before this beat is setup. Everything after pivots on it. If this transfiguration doesn't land—if the connection between violations and crime feels arbitrary or cute—the novel becomes a gimmick. It must feel *inevitable*. The reader should think: *of course*. Of course the man who sees what no one else sees is the man who was trained to see what no one wants to look at. The thematic resonance is that sanitation inspection is, at its core, the art of finding what is hidden behind surfaces—behind walls, under counters, inside pipes. That is also what criminal investigation is. Mace has always been a detective. He just didn't have a crime. Now he does, and the voice that was his affliction becomes his genius. This is the beat the audience will fall in love with him—and that love will make the later betrayal devastating.

---

## Beat 4: The Second Telling — Mace as Folk Hero, the Voice as Performance

**What needs to happen:** Mace's discoveries produce results—arrests, seizures, media coverage. The cable news cycle picks him up. He becomes a character: the Blue-Collar Sherlock, the Cleanest Man in Garland County. He is interviewed, profiled, memed. A consultancy offer materializes. Throughout this escalation, we remain inside his skull, and here is where the critical structural turn occurs: the inspection voice begins to *perform itself*. Mace starts cataloguing violations not only because he compulsively must, but because he knows it's what people want to hear. The monologue, previously involuntary and private, becomes a public act. He says the same things. He notices the same details. But there is a new audience inside his head—the camera, the follower count, the idea of himself as the character they love.

**The structural function:** This is Lispector's fourth beat—repetition with moral reframing. The inspection voice is materially identical, but the narrator's subject position has shifted. He has gone from *being* the voice to *wielding* it. The technique is palimpsest: the new version is written over the old, and both remain legible. The reader should experience a faint nausea of recognition—*the words are the same but something is wrong*. The comedy is still present (the specificity is still absurd and delightful), but it now has a performed quality, a too-polished sheen, like a joke told one too many times. The inner monologue, which was the most private and involuntary thing about Mace, has become his brand. This is the structural moment where the reader, if they are paying attention, realizes the voice is no longer a diagnostic instrument—it is a stage persona. And personas can be bought.

**Why this beat must hurt:** The satire here must cut in two directions simultaneously. Outward: at the culture that can only value a man's genuine obsession once it becomes entertaining content, that needs its heroes to be *characters*, that will watch a man's cognitive architecture and call it a bit. Inward: at Mace, who discovers that performing his own authenticity feels *better* than authenticity itself—more rewarding, more legible, more loved. The sheriff, crucially, should be visibly supportive during this phase. Encouraging. Proud. The reader should later understand that the sheriff was watching the inspection voice become performance and recognizing, with satisfaction, that a man who has learned to perform his own integrity has already begun to hollow it out.

---

## Beat 5: The Curdling — Corruption in the Same Voice

**What needs to happen:** Mace accepts his first payoff. Not in a dramatic scene of moral collapse—the opposite. It happens inside the inspection voice, mid-catalogue, as a *slight adjustment*. He is inspecting. He is noticing violations. And then he *doesn't record one*. The omission is almost imperceptible, narrated in the same obsessive stream: a rationalization that *sounds like* professional judgment. *The condensation on the prep surface is within acceptable variance given the ambient humidity and the seasonal adjustment factor—* but we know, and he half-knows, that this is the voice bent to a new purpose. The bribe was probably not even cash at first. A favor. A connection. Something that lets him keep doing what he loves. The stream continues—grease-trap readings, gasket conditions, sanitizer concentrations—and the corrupted entries are *woven in*, indistinguishable in tone from the righteous ones.

**The structural function:** This is the novel's deepest and most Lispectorian move: the same voice, the same syntax, the same obsessive specificity, now revealed as the *perfect instrument of self-deception*. The repetition that deepened understanding in Beats 1–3 now deepens corruption. The formal trick is that the reader must not be able to draw a clean line between Mace's earlier brilliance and his current rationalization—because there *is* no clean line. The cognitive machinery is identical. What made him see the cartel's traces is precisely what allows him to unsee his own compromise: the overwhelming flood of detail, the authority of the procedural voice, the genuine expertise that makes every excuse sound technically plausible. The reader, who was trained in Beat 2 to trust the inspection stream, now cannot tell which entries are honest. This is the banality of corruption—not a dramatic fall, but a contamination so gradual that the organism doesn't register the infection.

**Why this must be the hardest scene to write:** The temptation will be to signal the corruption clearly—to make Mace's rationalizations transparently hollow, to let the reader feel safely above him. This must be resisted absolutely. The rationalizations must be *genuinely persuasive*. The reader should find themselves nodding along, thinking *well, that IS within acceptable variance*, before catching themselves. The horror is not that Mace is lying. The horror is that he might not be—that the framework of sanitation scoring, which seemed like the last honest lens in a dishonest world, is flexible enough to accommodate almost anything. The thematic resonance: any moral system rigorous enough to be a religion is rigid enough to be gamed by its own priest. Mace games his own faith, and the scripture he cites is real.

---

## Beat 6: The Sheriff Revealed — The Broom That Sweeps the Kitchen Clean

**What needs to happen:** The identity of the criminal Mace could never quite find is revealed—to the reader, and belatedly and incompletely to Mace—as the county sheriff who has been beside him from the start. Every lead was fed. Every breakthrough was stage-managed. The sheriff needed a *visible, credible, obsessive* investigator to take down the sheriff's *competitors* within the cartel network while insulating the sheriff's own operation. Mace was not a detective. He was a weapon aimed by someone else. The violations were real. The crimes were real. The arrests were real. But the *selection*—which restaurants Mace was pointed at, which patterns he was encouraged to see—was the sheriff's architecture. The same structural principle as the cartel hiding distribution routes inside restaurant infrastructure: the sheriff hid his strategy inside Mace's obsession. And now, with Mace compromised by payoffs, he is the perfect fall. The sheriff withdraws support. The investigations into Mace begin. The cleanup starts.

**The structural function:** This is Lispector's broom—the ritualistic return to order that is more devastating than the chaos it follows. The sheriff is the narrative's cleaning agent. He sweeps up. The county returns to its surface normalcy: the visible cartel operation has been disrupted, arrests have been made, a corrupt inspector has been identified and will be prosecuted, and the system *appears* to have worked. narrative_story:
# The Cleanest Man in Garland County

## I.

The caulk along the backsplash had separated from the tile by three-sixteenths of an inch. Not uniformly—it bowed outward in the center like a lip pulling back from teeth, worst at the seam where the countertop met the wall behind the faucet, which was the exact place you'd expect failure given that every time you ran the tap, micro-splash deposited minerals on the silicone surface and the wet-dry cycle worked the bond loose over six to fourteen months depending on the product. He'd used DAP Kwik Seal in this kitchen. The Kwik Seal was rated for twenty-year adhesion under ideal conditions, but the conditions were not ideal because the conditions were never ideal, because conditions were a name people gave to entropy when they didn't want to admit entropy was winning.

Mace Pruitt stood in his underwear at 5:47 a.m. and stared at the caulk.

Behind the separation, he could not see mold. But he could not confirm the absence of mold. The gap created a capillary channel approximately one and a half millimeters wide, which was sufficient for moisture intrusion, which given the ambient humidity of Garland County, Arkansas, in July—averaging 78 percent at dawn, he'd checked—meant the probability of *Aspergillus niger* colonization behind the bead was not zero. It was in fact the kind of probability that a responsible person would treat as certainty, because the difference between "probably not yet" and "definitely yes" was a delta of about three weeks, and the difference between treating it now and treating it later was the difference between a razor blade and a caulk gun versus tearing out the backsplash to the cement board.

He picked up his coffee. Truck stop coffee, a Styrofoam cup from the Valero on 7 South. He'd bought it nine minutes ago. It had been dispensed at approximately 175°F, which he knew not from a thermometer but from the delay the machine imposed between the grinding cycle and the pour—the Bunn AXIOM machines at Valero stations held water at 200°F and the eight-second transit through the mixing chamber and the thermal loss to the Styrofoam knocked it down to a range of 170 to 180, depending on cup volume and whether the lid was on during the pour. His lid had not been on during the pour. He'd watched the girl behind the counter fail to position it before dispensing, which meant an additional three to five degrees lost to surface evaporation. So call it 172 when it hit his hand. That was nine minutes ago. Styrofoam's insulative properties meant a cooling rate of roughly 1.5 degrees per minute in a 74°F room. His kitchen was 74°F because the window unit was dying and he'd measured the output air at twelve degrees below ambient, which brought a 97-degree exterior down to only 85 at the vent and mixed to about 74 at the counter where he was standing because the thermal gradient in a single-wide was a function of—

The coffee was at 158.5°F. Give or take.

It should not be in Styrofoam. Polystyrene leaching began above 160°F under prolonged exposure, and while nine minutes was not prolonged, Mace did not care for the taste that the cup gave the coffee, which was a taste like plastic remembering it had once been petroleum, which it had. He should pour it into the ceramic mug that was sitting in the drying rack. The ceramic mug had been washed eleven hours ago with Dawn Professional at a concentration of approximately one tablespoon per gallon at a water temperature of—he'd used the hot tap, which on his water heater was set to 120°F, which was below the 171°F required for chemical-free sanitization under FDA Food Code Section 4-501.110, but the Dawn's surfactant action at that concentration compensated for the thermal deficit such that the mug could be considered acceptably clean by the standard of a private residence, though it would fail in a commercial establishment, which his kitchen was not, although he sometimes thought of it as one, or rather could not stop thinking of every kitchen as one, which was the problem, or had been the problem, or was the ongoing and apparently permanent condition of having been a health inspector for the Arkansas Department of Health for nineteen years and then not being one anymore.

He did not pour the coffee into the ceramic mug.

He drank it from the Styrofoam, standing at the counter in his underwear, and while he drank it he catalogued the kitchen—not voluntarily and not involuntarily but in the way that breathing was not voluntary and not involuntary, in the way that the lungs simply did what lungs did, which was the same way his eyes did what they did, which was: score.

The refrigerator: the gasket on the upper-right corner of the door was compressed unevenly, creating a seal failure of approximately two millimeters along a four-inch stretch, which meant cold air was bleeding out at a rate sufficient to cause the compressor to cycle 15 to 20 percent more frequently than necessary, which raised the internal temperature by one to two degrees, which placed the interior at an estimated 39 to 40°F, which was within the acceptable range of 32 to 41°F but trending upward. The gasket needed replacing. He'd noted this eleven days ago and had not replaced it because a replacement gasket for a Frigidaire FFTR1821QS cost $42.67 on Amazon and he had $113 in his checking account and the electric bill was $89 and the lot rent was due in six days.

The floor: vinyl composite tile, twelve-by-twelve, installed by the trailer's previous owner with a grout line of approximately one-eighth inch. Grout was discolored in the high-traffic path between the counter and the hallway—not mold, just ground-in dirt, clay-colored, the iron-rich soil of the Ouachitas tracking in on boots and never quite yielding to a mop. He mopped every third day with a 1:32 bleach solution. The solution was correct. The mop head was seven months old, which was four months past the point where a cotton mop head's filament structure degraded enough to reduce absorption by 30 percent. He needed a new mop head. The mop head cost $6.49 at the Dollar General on Albert Pike. He would buy the mop head. He would not replace the gasket. These were the kinds of decisions that constituted a life.

In the bathroom mirror, which he arrived at after walking eleven steps down the hallway, stepping over the buckled seam where two sections of subfloor no longer met flush—a trip hazard he'd reported to the park management in writing, three times, with photographs, using the language of OSHA 1910.22(a)(1), which governed walking-working surfaces, though OSHA did not technically govern residential trailer parks and the park management had told him this, twice, the second time without patience—

In the mirror: his face. Fifty-three years old. Skin that had been sun-damaged in the specific pattern of a man who'd spent two decades walking from his state-issued vehicle to the back entrances of restaurants in central Arkansas, meaning the left side more than the right because you always walked with the building on your right so you could see the dumpster enclosure and the grease-trap access on approach. His left temple had three actinic keratoses that a dermatologist had told him to watch. He watched them every morning. They did not change. His teeth were acceptable. His gums were receding at a rate consistent with age and with the fact that he'd been brushing with a medium-bristle toothbrush for thirty years because no one had corrected him until a dental hygienist in 2019 told him soft-bristle was the standard and he'd said, "Ma'am, I've been using medium for thirty years," and she'd said, "That's why your gums are receding," and he'd switched to soft but the damage, as with most damage, had already been structural.

His eyes were brown. They looked, even to him, like they were performing an audit.

He put on pants. He put on a shirt—short-sleeve button-down, pockets on both breasts, the kind of shirt a health inspector wore so he could carry a thermometer in one pocket and a pen in the other. He'd been buying this same shirt from the same rack at Walmart for nineteen years and had continued buying it after they let him go because it was the shirt he owned and because the pockets were useful and because he did not want to think about the third reason, which was that the shirt made him feel like a man who was going somewhere to do something that mattered.

He carried the thermometer in the left pocket. A ThermoWorks Thermapen ONE, $105, which he'd bought in 2021 when he still had savings and which was the single most expensive object in the trailer that was not the truck or the trailer itself. He carried it every day. He had not been employed as a health inspector for fourteen months. He carried it every day.

Outside: the truck, a 2007 Chevy Silverado with 214,000 miles and a check-engine light that had been on since 2022 and which indicated, according to the OBD-II scanner he'd borrowed from a neighbor, a P0420 code—catalytic converter efficiency below threshold—which was an emissions issue, not a drivability issue, which meant he could ignore it, except he could not ignore it, because it was a code, it was a failure, it was a system performing outside its designed parameters, and every time the light came on when he started the engine he felt the small familiar nausea of knowing something was wrong and doing nothing about it.

He started the engine. The light came on. The nausea arrived. He backed out of the lot.

On Albert Pike Road, heading toward the 7 intersection, he passed the Waffle House at mile marker 3 and noted automatically that the dumpster lid was open—a violation of the Arkansas Rules Pertaining to Food Establishments, Section 8-304.11, which required refuse receptacles to be closed when not in active use, which they never were at 6:02 a.m. because the morning shift didn't take out trash until after the breakfast rush, which meant the lid had been open since the night shift's last bag at approximately 11:30 p.m., which meant seven hours of access for rodents, raccoons, and feral cats, the latter of which were an established population in this stretch of Albert Pike because the motel behind the Exxon fed them, which was its own violation of basic sanitation principle though not technically covered under the food code because the motel was not a food establishment although they did offer a "continental breakfast" that Mace had once inspected and found to include a waffle iron with burned batter dating back, by colorimetric assessment of the carbonization, at least two weeks.

He noted the open dumpster lid the way he noted everything: with total clarity, total precision, and absolutely no authority to do anything about it.

---

## II.

The call came from Dale, who ran a handyman service out of a converted gas station on East Grand and who gave Mace work when he had it, which was intermittently, which was the only frequency at which Mace received anything anymore.

"Kitchen cleanup," Dale said. "Not a remodel. A restaurant that's transitioning ownership. New people want a deep clean before they take possession. I told them I had a guy who was particular."

"What restaurant?"

"The Jade Pearl. Used to be Jade Pearl Chinese, on the strip by the lake. The one with the green awning."

Mace knew the Jade Pearl. He'd inspected it twice during his tenure, in 2016 and again in 2019. In 2016, it had scored a 92—three minor violations involving the temperature of a buffet steam table, the absence of a hair restraint on a prep cook, and a handwashing sink that was accessible but blocked by a stack of bus tubs. In 2019, it scored an 87—the same steam table issue, which was now a repeat violation, plus a mouse dropping finding behind the dry storage shelving unit, plus a damaged ceiling tile above the dish area that showed water intrusion, plus a chemical storage issue where the sanitizer was shelved above the food prep area. He'd given the owner, a man named Tran who spoke limited English and called Mace "sir" in a way that made Mace feel simultaneously respected and guilty, a corrective timeline of fourteen days on the critical violations.

He'd never gone back for the re-inspection. Two months later, he was terminated.

The termination was officially a reduction in force. The state had consolidated the northwest and central districts, eliminated four field inspector positions, and kept the inspectors with seniority, of which Mace had plenty, and the inspectors who had not filed complaints about their supervisors' scoring inconsistencies, of which Mace had filed seven. The complaints were documented. The retaliatory termination was not. He'd been told by a lawyer in Little Rock that he had a case, probably, if he wanted to spend two years and $15,000 he didn't have. He did not have it. He drove home and sat in the parking lot of his trailer and stared at the check-engine light until it became a symbol of everything and then he went inside and mopped the floor with a 1:32 bleach solution and that was the end of his career.

He drove to the Jade Pearl.

It was worse than he expected, which meant it was approximately as bad as he'd calculated on the drive over, since his expectations and his calculations had diverged years ago. He expected, always, that things would be manageable. He calculated, always, that they would not.

The green awning was down on one side, the mount bolt having pulled free from the fascia board, which suggested either wind damage or rot in the wood behind the stucco, which was itself cracked in a branching pattern consistent with settling—the foundation on these lakeside strip-mall units was notorious for movement because the soil was Ozark shale mixed with fill dirt from the lake construction in the 1950s and had never been properly compacted. The cracking was cosmetic. Probably. Unless it extended through the substrate to the framing, in which case it was structural, and the damage behind the interior walls would be—

He went inside.

The smell hit him first, which was correct. Smell was always first. The nose processed olfactory data faster than the eye processed visual data; this was evolutionary, a survival mechanism, because the things that could kill you—spoilage gases, combustion byproducts, predator musk—often announced themselves chemically before they announced themselves visually. The smell in the Jade Pearl was a composite: rancid cooking oil, dominant, the unmistakable sour-sweet signature of lipid oxidation in a fryer that had not been drained and cleaned at closure; mildew, secondary, the wet-carpet note of *Stachybotrys* or *Cladosporium* growing somewhere with persistent moisture; and underneath both of these, faint but legible to a trained nose, the ammonia-adjacent sharpness of rodent urine, which meant the mouse problem from 2019 had not been addressed and had almost certainly escalated from mice to rats, because mouse populations in commercial kitchens followed a predictable arc from colonization to carrying-capacity crisis to displacement by *Rattus norvegicus*, which outcompeted *Mus musculus* in food-rich environments within eighteen to twenty-four months.

He set his bucket down. He had been hired to clean. He was, for the moment, unable to stop inspecting.

The kitchen: twelve-by-twenty, stainless steel prep tables bolted to the wall on the north side, a six-burner range with a wok station on the south, the walk-in cooler in the northwest corner, the three-compartment sink along the east wall. Standard Chinese-restaurant layout for a unit this size. He'd seen a hundred of them. He'd scored a hundred of them.

Walk-in cooler: he opened the door. The compressor was running—someone had left the power on, or the new owners had turned it on in advance of the transition. He pulled the Thermapen from his pocket and inserted the probe into the ambient air near the middle shelf.

52.4°F.

He stared at the readout. The acceptable range for a walk-in cooler was 32 to 41°F. At 52.4, every item in this unit was in the temperature danger zone and had been since—well, it was impossible to say since when, which was the problem with temperature abuse: without continuous monitoring, you could not determine the duration of the excursion, and without the duration, you could not assess the degree of risk, which meant you had to assume the worst, which was always total loss.

Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov)
The Azra Gambit
Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in.
